info.bio: Banda de Detroit.  1964 hasta finales de los 60.  Rob Tyner (cantante), Wayne Kramer y Fred Sonic Smith (guitarras) eran sus almas, custodiados por su propia guardia pretoriana compuesta por  Michael Davis (bajo)Dennis Thompson (batería). Tuvieron un comienzo prometedor, conocido especialmente por sus energéticas presentaciones, las que los llevaron a aparecer en la portada de la revista Rolling Stone en 1968, antes incluso de haber grabado su primer disco.

scenes.name: Protometal: volumen, distorsión y moteros
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Los precursores que aportan piezas sueltas del código: el volumen como estética (Blue Cheer, MC5), el sonido de guitarra grueso y distorsionado (los Kinks en «You Really Got Me»), la contundencia de los Who en directo (Townshend presume de que Live at Leeds engendró «ese objeto grosero y asqueroso que fue Led Zeppelin») y la iconografía motera de «Born to Be Wild» de Steppenwolf, cuyo verso «heavy metal thunder» dio nombre al género. Algunos críticos estadounidenses defienden a Iron Butterfly, Steppenwolf o Blue Cheer como primera banda de heavy. En 1971 la crítica ya usa el término: Mike Saunders, en Creem, dice que Sir Lord Baltimore domina «todos los trucos del heavy metal».

scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y sus herederos
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: La línea de art rock que reivindica el postpunk no es la del progresivo sinfónico sino la que va de The Velvet Underground al krautrock y al glam intelectual, fiel al principio minimalista «menos es más». Durante el «páramo» de los setenta, un racimo de espíritus afines unidos por su deuda con la Velvet (Lou Reed, John Cale, Nico, Iggy Pop, Bowie, Eno) colaboró en distintas combinaciones y sostuvo a los hipsters.

scenes.name: Detroit: MC5 y Stooges
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La ciudad más industrial de EE UU y cuartel de los elementos más extremistas de la contracultura: un rock'n'roll feroz y ruidoso se convierte en la voz de los obreros y de sus hijos. Los MC5 de John Sinclair, ala revolucionaria de las revueltas estudiantiles (Kick Out The Jams, «el equivalente rockero de una explosión nuclear»); los Stooges de Iggy Pop, síntesis de Chuck Berry, Rolling Stones, Velvet Underground y Doors que inventa el punk-rock («1970») y el voodoobilly («TV Eye»). Un nuevo rock'n'roll fundado en la violencia extrema.

podcast.title: Record Deal and Democratic National Convention (1968)
podcast.body: The MC5 secured a "big record deal" in 1968. Around the same time, they performed at the "ill-fated" Democratic National Convention in Chicago, appearing as guests of the White Panther Party. "Somehow they were signed to a big record deal in 1968. This was at around the same time as they appeared at the ill-fated Democratic National Convention in Chicago as guests of the White Panther Party."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early "Punk" Usage in Print (April 6, 1969)
podcast.body: A review of an album by this Detroit group, penned by rock writer Lester Banks and published in Rolling Stone magazine on April 6, 1969, contained an early and significant use of the word "punks" in a musical context. Banks described the group with the phrase "a bunch of 16-year-old punks on a meth power trip," marking an important step in associating the term with rebellious rock music. "In a review of an album by a Detroit group called the MC5, published in Rolling Stone magazine on April the 6th of 1969, he managed to use this phrase. A bunch of 16-year-old punks on a meth power trip."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inclusion on First Modern Picture Disc (1969)
podcast.body: MC5 was featured on what is considered the first modern-day picture disc, a compilation released by the German label Metronome in 1969, alongside The Doors. "a compilation of bands like the Doors and the MC5 released by a German label called Metronome in 1969."

podcast.title: Detroit Origins and Radical Politics (Mid-Late 1960s)
podcast.body: The MC5 was a Detroit-area group that emerged in the mid-to-late 1960s. They were known for being loud, profane, and highly political, embracing a "left-wing, super radical kind of way." "Another Detroit area group that made waves in the mid- and light 60s was the MC5."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Detroit's Raw Sound
podcast.body: In the late 1960s, as Detroit faced industrial crisis, racism, strikes, and police brutality, MC5 was one of the first bands to embody the city's tense social atmosphere. Unlike the psychedelic and spiritual rock prevalent elsewhere during the hippie movement, their sound became physical, raw, and violent, reflecting the city's turmoil. "Una de las primeras bandas en plasmarlo fue MC5."

podcast.title: Dropped by Record Label Due to Vulgar Letter
podcast.body: After releasing only one album under their new deal, the MC5 were dropped by their record company. This occurred because they wrote a vulgar letter on company letterhead and delivered it to record stores that had refused to stock their album. "Then they were dropped after they wrote a vulgar letter on company letterhead and delivered it to record stores that refused to stock their album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enhanced Street Cred from Controversies
podcast.body: Despite being dropped by their label for sending a vulgar letter, such stunts only served to enhance the MC5's "street cred" and rebellious image. "But of course, stunts like that only enhanced their street cred."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Exception to Garage Rock Decline
podcast.body: The MC5 were one of the bands that continued to be significant after the general decline of the original Garage Rock era around 1968. They are also considered a "Motor City ancestor" for the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, influencing later bands like The White Stripes and Yeah Yeah Yeahs. "The MC5, the band that eventually became Alice Cooper, to name 2."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Influential but Low-Selling
podcast.body: Despite never selling a large number of records, the band was tremendously influential on subsequent artists and movements due to their distinctive sound, radical attitude, and political views. "Never sold a lot of records, but they were tremendously influential with their sound and attitude and politics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Law Enforcement Harassment
podcast.body: The band frequently faced harassment from law enforcement due to their radical political views and touring activities. "They toured a lot, but they were always being hassled by law enforcement for their radical political views."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manager John Sinclair's Imprisonment
podcast.body: In 1969, the band's manager, John Sinclair, a member of the White Panthers, was sentenced to nearly 10 years in prison for giving two marijuana joints to an undercover female police officer. "Their manager, John Sinclair, was a member of the White Panthers. They lost him in 1969 when he was sentenced to almost 10 years, forgiving two joints to an undercover female police officer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Political Activism and FBI Surveillance
podcast.body: MC5 was closely aligned with the White Panthers, an extreme-left activist group advocating for the end of racism, drug legalization, anti-militarism, and the abolition of capitalism. Their radical political stance led to them being monitored by the FBI and banned by radio stations, yet they profoundly influenced a generation of musicians who recognized rock's potential as a political weapon and a form of organized protest. "El FBI los tenía fichados, las radios los vetaban, y a pesar de todo, marcar una toda una generación de músicos que entendió que el rock podía ser también un arma política y una forma de protesta organizada."

podcast.title: Political Progenitors of Punk
podcast.body: The MC5 are identified as "muck-raking progenitors" of punk rock, distinguished by their highly political stance. They represented an early example of bands using music for political expression, predating the more overtly class-conscious punk scene that emerged in the UK. "There were some muck-raking progenitors like the MC5, who were very political..."

podcast.title: Political Progenitors of Punk
podcast.body: The MC5 are identified as "muck-raking progenitors" of punk music. They were notably very political in their approach, differentiating them from the earlier, more artsy punk scene in New York. "There were some muck-raking progenitors like the MC5, who were very political."

srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy

podcast.title: Pre-Punk Pioneers
podcast.body: The MC5 is recognized as one of the most important pre-punk bands, known for their influential sound, attitude, and political stance. "He was one of the co-founders of Detroit's MC5, one of the most important pre-punk bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Proto-Punk and Political Activism (Mid-Late 1960s)
podcast.body: The MC5, a proto-punk band hailing from Detroit, was essentially an extension of the Marxist Black Panther Party, a militant socialist black nationalist organization that generated considerable controversy in the mid to late 1960s. The band further established an affiliated group known as The White Panthers. Despite their eventual internal political struggles that led to the band's dissolution, the MC5 effectively amplified the voices of marginalized people in the US during their active period. "The MC5, the Proto-Punk Band from Detroit, were essentially a wing of the Marxist Black Panther Party, a militant socialist black nationalist organization that stood up a lot of controversy in the middle of late 60s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sampled in KLF Song
podcast.body: Samples from MC5 were among at least eight distinct samples used in The KLF's massive 1990 single "What Time Is Love." "There were at least eight samples in this track, including from the MC5."
